metadata.topic: Aristotle's principle of correspondence (logoi to pragmata)
metadata.stance: Aristotle consistently holds a principle of truth as conformity of statements to extralinguistic reality, where logoi are causally dependent on pragmata; this is the only criterion for truth Aristotle recognizes and is central to understanding de Interpretatione 9.

label: Donini: Aristotle's counter-argument against determinism follows a parallel structure to

metadata.topic: Aristotle's response to determinism in de Interpretatione 9
metadata.stance: Aristotle's counter-argument against determinism follows a parallel structure to the deterministic argument: denying the futility of deliberation (c), then denying that everything happens by necessity (b), and finally denying wholesale application of bivalence/excluded middle to future singulars (a). The deterministic argument's fundamental flaw is that it violates the correspondence principle by moving from logoi to pragmata rather than vice versa.

label: Donini: The future's status as pragma is problematic for Aristotle's correspondence prin

metadata.topic: Status of future contingents as pragmata
metadata.stance: The future's status as pragma is problematic for Aristotle's correspondence principle; if the future is not a pragma in the same way as present/past, this affects whether truth can be spoken of concerning the future. Aristotle does not absolutely prohibit speaking of truth for the future, but restricts rather than abolishes the logical principle (ouk homoiōs, not oudamēs).

metadata.topic: Cyclical vs. linear time in Greek antiquity
metadata.stance: The cyclical conception of Greek time, popularized by Nietzsche's eternal return, has been challenged: cyclicity is not intrinsic to time itself but a feature of its measurement (following Aristotle), and linearity was also present in Greek culture from the archaic period onward.

label: Dihle: Greek philosophical theology from Plato and Aristotle onward did not conceive of

metadata.topic: Greek philosophical theology and divine will
metadata.stance: Greek philosophical theology from Plato and Aristotle onward did not conceive of divine will as arbitrary or unpredictable intention; rather, divine activity manifests perfect rationality, order, and beauty. The demiurge realizes only what reason shows to be possible and always chooses the best. No separate will spontaneously interferes with the rational programming of reality.
supporting_evidence: Cleanthes ap. Seneca Epistulae 41.1, Quaestiones naturales 2.35

label: Dihle: Jewish and early Christian theology conceived of creation as dependent solely on

metadata.topic: Jewish and Christian conception of divine will vs. Greek philosophy
metadata.stance: Jewish and early Christian theology conceived of creation as dependent solely on the arbitrary will of the divine creator, who could transform a lump of earth into any creature. This conception was preferable to Epicurean chance but incompatible with Greek rational cosmology. This fundamental difference between Greek and biblical thought becomes central to the historical development of the 'will' concept.
supporting_evidence: Galen De partibus corporis humani (on eyelashes and creation)

label: Dihle: Greek philosophical tradition, both Stoic and Platonic, rejected the popular rel

metadata.topic: Prayer and divine immutability in Greek philosophy
metadata.stance: Greek philosophical tradition, both Stoic and Platonic, rejected the popular religious notion that prayer could influence or change God's intention. Such change would imply imperfection, since God could not improve on his own rationality. Prayer served only to ascertain identity between cosmic and human reason (Stoics) or to contribute to fuller cognition of God (Platonists).
supporting_evidence: Cleanthes ap. Seneca Epistulae 41.1, Quaestiones naturales 2.35
